prompt: A portion of the human population believes that criminal behaviour has its roots in genes. Others think that circumstances lead people to commit crimes. Discuss your take on both views and put forward your opinions.
essay:
Whether criminal behaviour is inherited through genes or influenced by a person's surroundings has been a subject of debate. While some people believe that genetics play an important role in shaping human behaviour, others argue that social and environmental circumstances are the main causes of crime. I believe that although genes may influence certain personality traits, criminal behaviour is primarily the result of a person's upbringing, education, and living conditions.

Those who support the genetic theory argue that some individuals may inherit personality traits such as aggression, impulsiveness, or poor emotional control, which could increase the likelihood of engaging in criminal activities. According to this view, these inherited characteristics make certain people more prone to violence or antisocial behaviour than others. Supporters also point to scientific research suggesting that genetics can influence human behaviour to some extent. However, possessing these traits does not necessarily mean that a person will become a criminal.

On the other hand, many people believe that crime is largely influenced by external circumstances. Poverty, unemployment, lack of education, family violence, substance abuse, and negative peer pressure often push individuals towards illegal activities. Children who grow up in unstable families or crime-ridden neighbourhoods may consider criminal behaviour to be normal because of the environment in which they are raised. For example, a teenager who lacks educational opportunities and is surrounded by gangs is more likely to become involved in criminal activities than someone raised in a stable and supportive environment.

In my opinion, environmental factors play a much greater role than genetics in determining whether a person becomes a criminal. Even if someone has inherited aggressive tendencies, proper parenting, quality education, counselling, and positive social support can help them develop into responsible citizens. Likewise, many people with no genetic predisposition to violence may still commit crimes if they experience severe social or economic hardship. Therefore, governments should focus on improving education, reducing poverty, and strengthening family and community support systems to prevent crime.

In conclusion, although genetics may influence certain aspects of personality, I believe that criminal behaviour is mainly shaped by social and environmental circumstances. By addressing the root causes of crime through education, employment opportunities, and community support, society can reduce criminal behaviour more effectively than by focusing solely on genetic factors.
